title: The Great Works Course
about: An eleven-phase course through every work in README.md. Each phase has a core sequence (read in order) and a deeper shelf (the rest of that phase's sections, read as interest and time allow). Hour figures are rough reading-time estimates for the suggested portion of each work, not for complete editions.

phases.title: Tools of Thought
phases.intro: The medieval curriculum began with the language arts and the mathematical arts before any major author. This phase is short on purpose: learn the vocabulary of logic (genus, species, predication, syllogism), the parts of rhetoric, and the method of a geometric proof. Every later phase uses them.
questions: What is the difference between a valid argument and a true conclusion?
What are the five canons of rhetoric, and which one does modern writing neglect?
Why did Euclid's method become the model of certain knowledge for later philosophers?
phases.synthesis: In one page, explain how a medieval student would move from grammar to logic to rhetoric, and what each step equips them to do.

core.focus: Read it first; it was the standard primer before Aristotle. Learn the five predicables and note the unanswered question about universals.
The ten categories, with close attention to the account of primary and secondary substance in chapter 5.
On Interpretation 1-9, Prior Analytics I.1-7 (the syllogism), Posterior Analytics I.1-2, and Sophistical Refutations. Skim the Topics.
The five canons of rhetoric; Book III on the memory palace is the most cited section.
De Oratore Book I on the education of the orator. Brutus can wait for Phase 3.
Book I in full: definitions, postulates, common notions, then work each proposition through to I.47 (the Pythagorean theorem).

phases.title: The Greek World
phases.intro: Homer is the shared reference point for everything that follows in the Western sections. Read the poets, then the historians, then the philosophers, in roughly the order they wrote. Plato and Aristotle answer questions the tragedians and historians raised.
questions: What does Achilles want, and does he get it?
How do the tragedians treat the conflict between family obligation and the law of the city?
Thucydides and Plato both lived through the Peloponnesian War. What did each conclude from it?
How does Aristotle's account of the good life differ from Plato's?
phases.synthesis: Trace one idea (justice, fate, or the good life) from Homer through the tragedians to Plato and Aristotle.

core.focus: Iliad first. Mark Book 9 (the embassy), Book 18 (the shield), and Book 24 (Priam and Achilles). Then the Odyssey, tracking hospitality and homecoming.
Theogony for the genealogy of the gods; Works and Days for the ethic of labor and justice.
Read the Oresteia as one trilogy. The Eumenides ends a cycle of vengeance with a court at Athens.
Oedipus the King, Oedipus at Colonus, Antigone. Antigone sets divine law against the decree of the city.
Medea, Hippolytus, The Trojan Women, The Bacchae.
The Clouds first; its caricature of Socrates is the counterpart to Plato's portrait. Then The Frogs and Lysistrata.
Books I-II for method and digression, VII-IX for the Persian invasion.
Pericles' Funeral Oration (II.35-46), the plague (II.47-54), the Mytilenean debate (III.36-50), the Melian dialogue (V.84-116), the Sicilian expedition (VI-VII).
Heraclitus and Parmenides above all; the problem of change and permanence sets up Plato.
Suggested order: Gorgias, Phaedo, Symposium, Republic, Phaedrus, Timaeus. Leave the Laws for a later pass. The Apology and Crito, though not listed, are a short useful preface.
Nicomachean Ethics in full; then Politics I-III, Poetics, On the Soul II-III, Physics II, Metaphysics I and XII.

phases.title: Rome
phases.intro: Rome absorbed Greek learning and turned it toward law, duty, and empire. Read the historians of the Republic, then Cicero and the Augustan poets, then the imperial historians and the Stoics. Virgil and Cicero were the two Latin authors every later European student knew.
questions: What does Roman virtus mean, and how does it differ from Greek arete?
Is Aeneas admirable? What does Virgil suggest Rome cost?
How do Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius each practice Stoicism differently?
What does Tacitus think happened to Roman liberty?
phases.synthesis: Compare the Roman idea of duty in Cicero and Virgil with the Stoic idea of inner freedom in Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius.

core.focus: Book I for the method, Book VI for the mixed constitution that later shaped Montesquieu and the American founders.
Books I-V (founding to the Gallic sack) and XXI-XXX (the war with Hannibal).
Paired Lives: Theseus/Romulus, Lycurgus/Numa, Alexander/Caesar, Demosthenes/Cicero. Dip into the Moralia.
The Epicurean alternative: atoms, void, and no fear of death (Book III). Rediscovered in 1417.
On Duties first, then On Friendship and On Old Age; Tusculan Disputations I and V; a selection of the Letters.
The closing myth of Cicero's On the Republic. It links Roman public service to Platonic cosmology.
Books 1-6 (Troy to the underworld), then 7-12 (the war in Italy). Compare Book 6 with Odyssey 11.
Odes I-III, a few Epistles, and the Ars Poetica.
The Metamorphoses in full; much later poetry and painting depend on it.
Letters 1-30 and On the Shortness of Life.
Agricola and Germania (both short), then Annals I-VI on Tiberius.
Julius, Augustus, Tiberius, Nero. Compare his method with Tacitus.
The Enchiridion, then Discourses Book I. Chapter 1 of the Enchiridion is the core distinction.
Read slowly, one book per sitting. Book 1 lists what he learned from each teacher.
The only Latin novel to survive complete. Book 11 on the Isis mysteries anticipates Phase 4's conversion narratives.

phases.title: Scripture and the Early Church
phases.intro: The Hebrew Bible and the New Testament, followed by the writers who defined Christian doctrine in contact with Greek philosophy. Plotinus is placed here because Augustine read him before his conversion. Read the Psalms a few at a time across the whole phase.
questions: How does the God of Genesis and Exodus differ from the gods of Homer and Hesiod?
What question does Job ask, and is it answered?
What did the Fathers take from Plato, and what did they reject?
How does Augustine's City of God answer the fall of Rome?
phases.synthesis: Write on Augustine as the meeting point of Phase 2 (Plato and Plotinus), Phase 3 (Rome and Cicero), and Scripture.

core.focus: Genesis and Exodus closely; Leviticus through Deuteronomy at a steadier pace.
Spread across the phase: a few each day.
The frame story, the dialogues, and the speeches from the whirlwind (38-41).
Ecclesiastes against Proverbs: the same tradition in two moods.
Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos. Note the demand for justice and the promise of restoration.
Mark first, then Matthew, Luke, and John. Note what John includes that the other three do not.
Paul's speech at Athens (17:16-34) meets Phase 2 directly.
Romans, 1 Corinthians (chapters 13 and 15), Galatians, Philippians.
Read after Daniel if possible; the imagery draws on it.
The earliest surviving church manual: the Two Ways, baptism, the Eucharist.
The Letter to the Romans, written on the way to his execution.
The First Apology and its idea of the logos spermatikos in pagan philosophy.
Book I on the Gnostic systems, then Books III-IV on apostolic tradition and recapitulation.
On the Incarnation in full; The Life of Antony founded the genre of the desert saint.
I.6 (On Beauty), V.1, and VI.9 (On the Good or the One). These are the 'books of the Platonists' Augustine mentions in Confessions VII.
Books I-IX narrative, X on memory, XI on time.
City of God I-V, XI-XIV, XIX. On Christian Doctrine Book II for how the tradition read texts.
The Prologue and chapters on obedience, humility (7), and daily order. It governed Western monasticism.
The Mystical Theology is very short: the source of the negative way used in Phases 5 and 8.

phases.title: The Middle Ages
phases.intro: Three strands interleaved: the northern heroic literature (Anglo-Saxon, Norse, Celtic), the theology of the schools and cloisters, and the romance and epic that culminated in Dante and Chaucer. Boethius opens the phase because every medieval writer knew him.
questions: How does the heroic code of Beowulf and the sagas change once Christianity arrives?
What is scholastic method, and why does Aquinas write in questions and objections?
How does courtly love in the romances relate to love of God in the mystics?
What does Dante's structure (three realms, 100 cantos) say about his view of order?
phases.synthesis: Compare a Germanic hero (Beowulf or Njal) with a romance knight (Gawain or Lancelot) and with Dante the pilgrim.

core.focus: Written in prison awaiting execution. Book II on Fortune's wheel, Book V on providence and free will.
Book II.13 (the sparrow in the hall) and IV.24 (Caedmon).
The poem's three fights and its Christian narrator commenting on a pagan past.
The Wanderer and The Seafarer first; The Dream of the Rood recasts the Crucifixion in heroic diction.
Voluspa (the creation and end of the world) and Havamal (the sayings of Odin), then the heroic poems.
Njal's Saga first. Law, feud, and the conversion of Iceland.
Cu Chulainn's defense of Ulster; the central epic of the Ulster Cycle.
The Four Branches first, then Culhwch and Olwen for the earliest Arthur.
Compare Roland's pride with Achilles'. Oliver is the counterweight.
Proslogion 2-4 (the ontological argument) and Cur Deus Homo.
Historia Calamitatum; the prologue to Sic et Non sets out the method of reconciling authorities.
On Loving God: the four degrees of love.
Yvain and Lancelot, then Perceval, the first Grail story.

core.match: 7:Anon. — Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
core.focus: The three temptations and the three blows.
Summa Theologiae I qq.1-13 (God, including the five ways in q.2), I-II qq.90-97 (law), selections on the virtues in II-II; On Kingship.
A short itinerary of the mind's ascent in six stages, set against Aquinas.
The Divine Comedy in order. Many readers stop after Inferno; Purgatorio and Paradiso are where the argument resolves.
The General Prologue, then the Knight's, Miller's, Wife of Bath's, Pardoner's, and Nun's Priest's Tales.
The negative way from Pseudo-Dionysius put into English practice.
The first woman known to have written a book in English. The parable of the lord and the servant (ch. 51).
The Tale of the Sankgreal and the last two tales: the fall of the Round Table.
Books I-II. It closes the phase as the late-medieval devotional handbook.

phases.title: Judaism and Islam
phases.intro: The rabbinic tradition and the Islamic world: scripture, law, commentary, philosophy, and Persian and Arabic poetry. The medieval Arabic philosophers transmitted and extended Aristotle, which is why they sit next to Phase 5's scholastics. Maimonides belongs to both traditions here.
questions: How does rabbinic argument (dispute preserved, not resolved) compare with scholastic method?
What are the central themes of the Qur'an, and how is it organized?
What is at stake between al-Ghazali and Averroes on philosophy and revelation?
What does Sufi poetry mean by love, and how does it compare with Phase 5's mystics?
phases.synthesis: Set Maimonides, Averroes, and Aquinas side by side on the relation of reason and revelation.

core.focus: The ethical sayings of the rabbis and the chain of transmission from Sinai.
Selected tractates: Berakhot, Shabbat, Sanhedrin.
Selections with a guide. Watch how a single Mishnah passage unfolds into layered debate.
Genesis Rabbah read alongside Genesis.
Rashi on Genesis: the standard commentary printed beside the Torah text.
A translation with notes. One common approach: the short Meccan suras at the end first, then from the beginning.
The earliest surviving biography of Muhammad, in Ibn Hisham's recension.
A compact entry into the hadith literature. Hadith 2 (Gabriel) summarizes the faith.
Pre-Islamic odes: the deserted campsite, the journey, the boast.
Plato's Republic reimagined with a philosopher-prophet as ruler.
Selections: the metaphysics of necessary being and the 'floating man' argument from the Book of Healing.
Deliverance from Error first (his autobiography), then the Incoherence of the Philosophers.
The Decisive Treatise, then selections from the Incoherence of the Incoherence answering al-Ghazali.
A child raised alone on an island reasons his way to God. Often compared with Robinson Crusoe.
The introduction, Part I on divine attributes, and Part III on providence and the reasons for the commandments.
A king questions a philosopher, a Christian, a Muslim, and a rabbi. A counterpoint to Maimonides.
An abridged translation. The story of Rostam and Sohrab is the best-known episode.
The birds' journey through seven valleys to the Simorgh.
Masnavi Book I, beginning with the song of the reed.
The Gulistan: prose and verse anecdotes of conduct.
A selection of ghazals. Goethe's West-Eastern Divan (not on this list) was written in response to him.
The frame tale of Shahrazad and a selection; note the nested stories.
The theory of asabiyya (group solidarity) and the rise and fall of dynasties.
A modern bridge: the I-Thou and I-It relations.

phases.title: India, China, and Japan
phases.intro: Three linked traditions. India first (Veda, Upanishads, epics, early Buddhism), then China (Confucian and Daoist classics, poetry), then Buddhism's development through Madhyamaka and Chan into Japanese Zen and the warrior literature. The later sections of this phase assume the earlier ones.
questions: What do the Upanishads mean by atman and brahman, and how does the Buddha's teaching of anatta respond?
What does Krishna tell Arjuna about action and its fruits?
Where do Confucius and Laozi agree, and where do they part?
How does Zen's emphasis on direct experience relate to the sutras it inherited?
phases.synthesis: Compare the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on action with the Stoics (Phase 3) and with the Hagakure.

core.focus: Selected hymns, including the Creation Hymn (X.129) and the Purusha hymn (X.90).
Isha and Katha first (short), then Chandogya VI (tat tvam asi) and Brihadaranyaka.
Read twice: once for the story, once for the three yogas of action, knowledge, and devotion.
An abridged translation is standard for a first reading.
An abridgment. The Gita sits inside it; now read it in context.
Digha Nikaya 2 and 16 (the Buddha's last days); Majjhima Nikaya 22 (the raft) and 63 (the poisoned arrow).
Short verses on the Theravada path.
The eight limbs, with a commentary.
Chapters 1, 18, 24, 25 with a commentary. Emptiness and the two truths.
One page: 'form is emptiness, emptiness is form.'
Short. The oldest dated printed book (868) is a copy of it.
Chapter 6 (patience) and chapter 8 (exchanging self and other).
Ren (humaneness), li (ritual), the junzi (gentleman).
The four sprouts (2A6) and the claim that human nature is good.
Compare two translations; they diverge widely.
The Inner Chapters (1-7): the butterfly dream, Cook Ding.
Short. Winning without fighting; knowing yourself and the enemy.
The structure of the 64 hexagrams and the Great Commentary (Xici).
A selection; Confucius is said to have compiled it.
With Li Bai, the two poets of the high Tang. Du Fu writes war and displacement.
The poetry contest for the patriarchate and the teaching of sudden awakening.
Forty-eight koans. Case 1 (Zhaozhou's Mu) is the classic first koan.
Fukanzazengi, then the Genjokoan and Uji (Being-Time) fascicles of the Shobogenzo.
The first third at least; an abridgment is acceptable for a first reading.
Opens on impermanence (the bell of Gion). The Genpei War.
Short essays on impermanence and taste.
Travel prose with haiku. Read slowly.
Letters to a swordsman on the mind that does not stop.
The Water and Void books.
A selection; it was compiled from conversations c. 1716.

phases.title: Renaissance and the New Science
phases.intro: The recovery of ancient texts (including the Hermetic writings, then believed older than Moses), the new political realism, the essay and the stage, and the reordering of the cosmos by Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and Newton. The phase ends with the philosophers who tried to rebuild knowledge on new foundations.
questions: What did Renaissance thinkers believe they were reviving?
Is Machiavelli describing politics or recommending it?
What changed in how people knew things between Aquinas and Descartes?
How do Hobbes and Locke differ on the state of nature?
phases.synthesis: Choose one work from Phase 2 and follow its revival and transformation in this phase.

core.focus: The sonnet sequence that set the European lyric. A selection is enough.
Corpus Hermeticum I (Poimandres) and XIII; the Emerald Tablet. Ficino translated them in 1463.
The Oration: the human being as the creature with no fixed place.
The Prince, then Discourses Book I. The Discourses show his republicanism.
Book I (the debate on counsel) matters as much as Book II (the island).
'That to philosophize is to learn to die', 'Of cannibals', 'Of experience', and the 'Apology for Raymond Sebond'.
Both parts. Part II (1615) responds to Part I's readers and to a spurious sequel.
Richard II, Henry IV Parts 1-2, Henry V; then Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth.
An infinite universe with innumerable worlds. Burned in Rome in 1600.
The dedication to Pope Paul III and Book I.
Selections on the ellipse (Astronomia Nova) and the third law (Harmonices Mundi V).
The First and Second Days.
Novum Organum Book I (the four idols) and a handful of the Essays.
Discourse on Method, then all six Meditations.
Parts I and II. Chapter 13 on the state of nature.
The wager (Lafuma 418), the two infinities, and the 'thinking reed'.
Books I-IV and IX-XII. Compare the epic invocation with Homer and Virgil.
Parts I and V with a guide; the geometric method from Phase 1 applied to God and ethics.
Definitions and laws of motion, the Rules of Reasoning at the start of Book III, and the General Scholium.
Second Treatise of Government in full; Essay Book II on ideas.

phases.title: Enlightenment to the Twentieth Century
phases.intro: The critique of reason and its limits, the political revolutions and their critics, evolution, the unconscious, and the physics of the twentieth century. The phase ends with the mid-century thinkers who wrote after the world wars.
questions: What does Kant mean by a Copernican revolution in philosophy?
Burke and Tocqueville both study revolution. What does each fear?
What does Nietzsche mean by the death of God, and who else in this phase is answering the same problem?
How did Darwin and the new physics change the questions philosophers asked?
phases.synthesis: Trace the modern answer to 'what is a human being?' from Hume and Kant through Darwin, Freud, and Heidegger.

core.focus: Ninety short sections; the best possible world.
The Elements (axioms) and the three ages of gods, heroes, and men.
Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding in full; Treatise Book I Part IV on personal identity.
Books I-VIII on the three forms of government and Book XI on the separation of powers.
Candide, written in answer to Leibniz.
The Social Contract; the first books of Emile and the Confessions.
Theory of Moral Sentiments Part I first, then Wealth of Nations Book I.
Groundwork first; then the two Prefaces, Introduction, and Transcendental Aesthetic of the first Critique.
Written in 1790, before the Terror. His argument on inherited institutions.
Volume I Part II ch. 7 (tyranny of the majority); Volume II Part IV on soft despotism.
The Preface and the lordship-and-bondage section (paras. 178-196) of the Phenomenology, then the Philosophy of Right.
World as Will Book IV, then a selection of the Essays.
Fear and Trembling on Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 22 from Phase 4).
The 1844 Manuscripts on estranged labor; Capital Volume I, chapter 1 and Part VIII.
Origin chapters 1-4 and 14 (recapitulation and conclusion).
Birth of Tragedy (it returns to Phase 2), Genealogy essay I, Gay Science 125 (the madman).
The Varieties: lectures on the sick soul, conversion, and mysticism.
Civilization and Its Discontents in full; Interpretation of Dreams chapter 2.
Memories, Dreams, Reflections first, then Answer to Job (after Phase 4's Job).
Einstein's own popular account. Part I (special relativity).
The Copenhagen interpretation and his comparison with Greek natural philosophy.
The 1943 lectures that influenced the discovery of DNA's structure.
Introduction and Division I with a guide; Division II on death and authenticity.
The Tractatus (short, dense), then Investigations sections 1-133.
Gravity and Grace is a compilation of notebook entries; read slowly.
The Human Condition: labor, work, and action. Origins Part III if time allows.

phases.title: The Modern Imagination
phases.intro: The novel, the lyric, and the drama of the last three centuries, read now because they respond to everything before them. Tolstoy and Dostoevsky answer Phase 9; Joyce rewrites the Odyssey; Eliot's Four Quartets draws on Phase 5's mystics; Tolkien draws on Phase 5's Norse and Anglo-Saxon material.
questions: What can the novel do that epic and tragedy could not?
How do Dostoevsky and Nietzsche respond differently to the same crisis?
Which ancient or medieval works does each modern writer rewrite?
How do the twentieth-century writers treat war?
phases.synthesis: Pick one modern work and map its sources back through at least three earlier phases.

core.focus: Faust Part One in full; Part Two in selection.
Paired poems: The Lamb and The Tyger.
The 1802 Preface to Lyrical Ballads, 'Tintern Abbey', and Prelude Books I-II.
Pride and Prejudice, then Emma.
A novel in verse; the founding work of Russian literature.
Read the cetology chapters; they carry the book's argument.
Madame Bovary: Emma's reading shapes her life.
The Death of Ivan Ilyich first, then Anna Karenina, then War and Peace.
Notes from Underground, Crime and Punishment, The Brothers Karamazov (the Grand Inquisitor: Book V ch. 5).
Middlemarch in full; the Finale is essential.
Zarathustra's Prologue, then Beyond Good and Evil Parts 1 and 9.
'The Lady with the Dog', 'Ward No. 6'; The Cherry Orchard.
Heart of Darkness first.
The Metamorphosis, then The Trial.
The First and Ninth Elegies.
Swann's Way; continue if it holds.
Portrait first. Read Ulysses with a chapter guide after the Odyssey (Phase 2).
Death in Venice, then The Magic Mountain.
The Waste Land with its notes; Four Quartets draws on The Cloud of Unknowing and Julian of Norwich.
Orthodoxy: a defense of belief against the thinkers of Phase 9.
The Abolition of Man (on the Tao across traditions) and Till We Have Faces (Cupid and Psyche from Apuleius, Phase 3).
Storm of Steel: a German infantry officer's memoir of the Western Front.
The Stranger, then The Myth of Sisyphus.
One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich first; The Gulag Archipelago in the one-volume abridgment.
The Hobbit, then The Lord of the Rings. Note what it borrows from Beowulf, the Eddas, and the Kalevala.

phases.title: Capstone: The Forbidden Shelf
phases.intro: Works associated with controversial or extremist positions, placed last so they can be read against the full tradition they argue with. Recommended preparation: Plato's Republic, Hobbes, Burke, Hegel, Marx, and Nietzsche. Read each alongside a critical introduction or a serious critic, and note which earlier works each author claims or distorts.
questions: Which earlier work does each author claim as precedent, and is the reading faithful?
What does each author take to be the root problem of modernity?
Where does each argument depend on an assumption it does not defend?
phases.synthesis: Choose one author and write the strongest response to them from within the earlier phases.

core.focus: The interpolated pamphlet 'Yet Another Effort, Frenchmen' states the political argument.
Considerations on France (1797): providence and the Revolution. Read against Burke.
Egoism against Feuerbach and Hegel. Marx and Engels answered it in The German Ideology.
The theory of the political myth of the general strike.
The Introduction and the morphology of cultures. Compare with Vico and Ibn Khaldun.
The friend-enemy distinction; sovereignty as the decision on the exception. Compare with Hobbes.
Revolt Against the Modern World Part I. Note how he uses Phase 7 and the Hermetic sources.
Aphorisms. Compare with Pascal and Schopenhauer.
